title: How to judge (and minimise) the risk of using sensitive information with an AI chatbot
content:
One of the most common misunderstandings about large language models (LLMs) is the idea that if you upload a document such as an interview transcript, confidential leak or sensitive dataset to an AI tool like ChatGPT, it might reveal that document to another user.

There are no publicly documented cases of this happening.

The reason for this is the same reason why AI shouldn’t be treated as a search engine: large language models like GPT-5 don’t work by retrieving documents for users — they work by separating documents into parts of language (‘tokens’ in the jargon), adding those to a vast ocean of other tokens, and training on a database of relationships between those.

When you ask a question like “Who is the CEO of Apple?” a genAI tool doesn’t retrieve information from a document. Instead it breaks down your question into tokens like “CEO” and “Apple” and “Who”, calculates the most statistically likely meaning of those things (e.g. is that apple probably a fruit or a company), and then the most statistically likely sequence of words which might form a meaningful answer to that question.

title: How data journalism is done on TikTok: six key takeaways from watching 50 videos
content:
Short-form vertical video is quickly becoming a key format for telling all types of news stories — and data journalism is no exception.

As a data journalist, I wanted to know how these outlets use this new and evolving digital video format to create “data shorts”: short-form social media videos in a vertical, reel-style format, that analyses or reports on specific datasets or newly released data.

I analysed 50 data shorts from the TikTok accounts of five major UK news publications — the BBC, ITV News, Guardian, Times and Financial Times — to examine how these digital news outlets approach the format. I looked at the genre of story they covered, the angles they focused on, their length, and their use of animation, to help inform my guidelines.

My analysed data shorts averaged a runtime of just under 84 seconds.

The BBC ranked lowest for average video length, at just under a minute, while the Financial Times had the highest at 105 seconds.

Notably, none of the publications had an average video length over two minutes, despite TikTok allowing longer uploads up to 60 minutes.
